title: The other half
hook: Aristophanes' myth: humans split in two, searching for their other half (Symposium 189–193)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was eros, love as longing, climbing Diotima's ladder. Your line was the ladder. Today, the same dinner party, and a very different speech.

Earlier that night at the Symposium, before Socrates speaks, it's the comic playwright Aristophanes' turn, and he has the hiccups. A doctor at the table tells him to hold his breath, then to gargle with water, and if all else fails, to tickle his nose and sneeze. The doctor speaks in his place while he recovers. When Aristophanes finally gets the floor, he tells the evening's strangest story, and maybe the easiest one to remember.

First, round people. Long ago, Aristophanes says, humans were round, with four arms, four legs and two faces looking opposite ways. They ran by rolling along like tumblers turning cartwheels. There were three kinds: male, female, and a kind that was both. Second, cut in two. They grew so strong and bold that they tried to climb up and attack the gods. Zeus didn't wipe them out; he cut each one in half, and Apollo turned their faces around and drew the skin together at the navel, a mark left as a reminder. Third, the search. Ever since, each half longs for its other half. When two find each other, they don't want to be apart even for a moment, though neither can say exactly what they want. Love is the name for that desire and pursuit of the whole. Fourth, a comedy, and an answer. It's a playwright's story, told with a wink, and Plato doesn't give it the last word: later that night, Diotima says love isn't of a half or a whole unless it is good. Still, the picture has lasted. Some readers hear in it something they know: meeting a person and recognizing them.
screen: `ROUND PEOPLE.` · `CUT IN TWO.` · `THE SEARCH.` · `A COMEDY, AND AN ANSWER.` · then, large: `THE OTHER HALF.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who supplies something you lack: a partner, a friend, a sister or brother, a teacher; it doesn't have to be romance. Breathe in and let their face come; breathe out and notice one thing they bring that you don't. Stay with that for a while, without needing to explain it.
Aristophanes. The comic playwright whose myth of round people, cut in two, became an answer to what love searches for. Today's word.
Your line: the half. A comic myth, and a picture that has lasted. Day eight hundred twenty-one, done.

howItsDone: Aristophanes' myth from Plato's Symposium is read in philosophy and literature classes, and its picture of searching for one's other half turns up in writing about love; readers take it as comedy, as a myth, or both.

chat.says: Where does the idea of finding your other half come from?
options: From Aristophanes' comic myth in Plato's Symposium: round people Zeus cut in two.
From Diotima, who taught Socrates that love always seeks its missing half.
From a modern dating slogan; no ancient writer ever pictured it that way.
chat.meaning: In the Symposium, Aristophanes tells of round people Zeus cut in half. Love is the name for the desire and pursuit of the whole.

Aristophanes.meaning: a comic playwright at Plato's dinner party

Symposium.meaning: Plato's dialogue set at a dinner party of speeches on love

Zeus.meaning: in the myth, the god who cut each round person in two

Apollo.meaning: in the myth, the god who drew the skin together at the navel

Diotima.meaning: the wise woman whose speech answers Aristophanes later that night

notes: All of Plato paraphrased. 'Desire and pursuit of the whole' echoes Jowett's wording at 192e; unquoted here. Confirm.
The doctor is Eryximachus; his remedies (hold breath, gargle, sneeze) at 185d–e. Confirm he speaks in Aristophanes' place.
Three kinds (male, female, androgynous) at 189d–e; the navel as a reminder at 190e–191a. Confirm.
Diotima's reply at 205d–e is phrased loosely ('love isn't of a half or a whole unless it is good'); confirm.
The myth concerns same-sex as well as opposite-sex pairs; the script keeps the practice open to any kind of bond.

Audit: no changes. Hiccups and Eryximachus's remedies, round people (four arms, four legs, two faces, cartwheels), three kinds, the attack on the gods, Apollo and the navel, and Diotima's reply at 205e all checked against the text.
